label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: You can read both. That is the point:
findings.why: A 'That is the point' opening, and the narrator states the moral instead of speaking as the editor with hindsight.

findings.quote: a team of agents you cannot read is a team you cannot trust.
findings.why: A general maxim reported from nowhere, with no 'I' and no moment in the editor's day.

findings.quote: That is a strong position precisely because it is a narrow one
findings.why: The narrator reports and assesses the role without saying what the editor thought or did at the time.

findings.quote: three greyed cards: the storyteller, the talk's story
findings.why: As a busy reader I get three roles in one clause-run with no sense of what each did; the figure carries what the text skips, and the text then says 'you will meet them properly'.

findings.quote: checks first and last in every run; reviews of the pinned tools
findings.why: 'Pinned tools' and 'run' are used before being explained, and security is the role I most want to copy.

findings.quote: A scope is a list in a file. A check reads the list and flags any change outside it.
findings.why: The scope is defined at line 25 and again here, and the quoted slide line says the same a third time.

findings.quote: something you expect, something that checks, or something that locks.
findings.why: A triad closing the exercise, and 'look at ... and note' is an instruction on how to read; the three terms are not set up earlier in the chapter.

findings.quote: each with what it cost and whose own record says so.
findings.why: Good promise, but nine entries each with two italic labels and a cost line make the chapter feel like a form on a phone.
Two entries (lock, parts) are a pointer plus a one-line quote, restating the cost line just above them; a reader on a phone gets a stub.

findings.quote: The request landed between the storyteller's sessions, its next turn came after the deadline
findings.why: Reads as a report of the record with no 'I'; the storyteller's own line at 56 then says it again.

findings.quote: it was nothing sensitive, an agent that got a bit excited
findings.why: Reassures rather than explains, and for a team about to copy the pattern, what the redaction check was is exactly the missing takeaway.

findings.quote: nobody carried the correction back in
findings.why: Strong story and a usable lesson for my team, but told as the record's account; the editor's own 'I' only appears for the freeze, not for what he felt or would change.

findings.quote: The designer wrote what had been planned, not what had happened
findings.why: Said by the narrator and then again by the designer in the next line ('I wrote the plan down as if it were the fact').

findings.quote: If you keep one, keep it where your agents will read it.
findings.why: An instruction to the reader; it is the one concrete takeaway in the chapter and deserves more than a closing line.

findings.quote: You met all nine at the start of the book.
findings.why: Presumes I remember nine roles from earlier; a phone reader dipping in cannot, and a one-line reminder of who is who would help.

findings.quote: made the gate read every session's record
findings.why: 'Gate' is used without explanation here, and each answer leans on terms (wake, hold, lock, gate) I would have to have kept from earlier chapters.

findings.quote: a second reading, not a second identity
findings.why: The same phrase is repeated at line 113; it is a good line used twice, the second time as the chapter's close.

what_holds: 06-roles-as-a-cast-you-can-read.md: the contrast between a scope as a setting and a boundary is the most copyable idea in the three sections, and the slide's own quoted line makes it stick.
06-roles-as-a-cast-you-can-read.md: security shown as a card with nothing on it but 'proposed' is an honest and memorable way to say a control was planned and never staffed.
17-what-did-not-work.md: the correction lost in the freeze, with its small-error framing and 'write down what is waiting to go in when it is unfrozen', is a rule I could use tomorrow.
17-what-did-not-work.md: the 'what it cost / whose record' pairing gives each failure a consequence, which is what my team would need to judge the risk.
17b-the-members-look-back.md: the two-answer format per member is quick to scan between meetings, and security having no interview because the historian would not invent one is a trust-builder.
notes: As a busy team member with agents of my own, the takeaway I want is a short pattern I could copy: a page of rules and a checkable policy per agent, a hold anyone can pull, a list of misses. It is there but scattered across sections and the reader has to assemble it. A method that leans on one central conductor is my deal-breaker: the conductor carries a great deal here, and 17b admits its reviewers shared its reach, so the sections do not yet answer whether a team without a conductor could do this.
